summary: The Chery E5 (rebranded from Omoda E5 during 2025, with the Omoda name now reserved for a separate model line) is one of the cheapest new electric SUVs on sale in Australia, a small front-wheel-drive EV pitched on price and standard equipment rather than dynamic polish. Australian reviewers consistently praise its value, long warranty and well-equipped cabin, but mark it down for unsettled ride quality, an over-cautious safety-assist calibration, and a boot that trails class rivals. The range is a single Ultimate grade ($35,990 before on-roads, advertised nationally from $37,990 drive-away but $39,604 drive-away for a Melbourne postcode) with a 58.9kWh LFP battery and 430km WLTP range; a facelifted MY27 'New E5' is listed as coming soon but is not yet priced or orderable.
pros: One of the cheapest new electric SUVs on sale in Australia at $35,990 before on-roads, undercutting the BYD Atto 3 ($39,990) and Geely EX5 ($41,990)
Long ownership package: 7-year unlimited-km vehicle warranty and 8-year unlimited-km battery warranty, plus 7-year capped-price servicing
Well-equipped single grade: dual 12.3-inch screens, heated front and rear seats, heated steering wheel, Sony audio, power tailgate, sunroof and a full-size spare
430km WLTP range from a 58.9kWh LFP battery, with a heat pump and 155kW motor (0-100km/h in 7.6 seconds)
cons: Softly sprung, with body lean in corners and sharp bumps such as expansion joints upsetting the ride; reviewers split on whether it is jittery or comfortable around town
Safety-assist calibration is poor: lane centring that cannot hold the lane and can steer toward other vehicles, and a driver monitor that chimes at normal glances
Small 300-litre boot (to the cargo cover, seats up) trails the Atto 3's 440 litres and the Jaecoo J5 EV's 384 litres
Slow DC charging for the class: 80kW peak, about 30 minutes for 30-80%, and only 6.6kW single-phase AC
A facelifted MY27 E5 is listed as coming soon, so a current car may depreciate faster once it arrives
